issues.title: Things to check
issues.empty-input: We couldn't find any directive in this text.
issues.violation-message: This is an error message, not your policy. It only shows the rule that blocked something ({directive}). Find the whole policy, then paste it here.
issues.violation-message-unnamed: This is an error message, not your policy. It only shows the rule that blocked something. Find the whole policy, then paste it here.
issues.unknown-directive: "{directive}" isn't a CSP directive, so browsers ignore it. Is it a typo?
issues.duplicate-directive: "{directive}" appears more than once. Browsers only use the first one and ignore the rest.
issues.deprecated-directive: "{directive}" is deprecated or has no effect in modern browsers.

deprecated.report-uri: "report-uri" is the older way to receive violation reports. It still works, and browsers that don't support report-to yet only report through it: keep it, and add report-to beside it.
deprecated.prefetch-src: "prefetch-src" was removed from the specification and current browsers ignore it. You can delete it.
deprecated.block-all-mixed-content: "block-all-mixed-content" is obsolete: browsers now upgrade or block insecure content on secure pages by themselves. You can delete it.
deprecated.plugin-types: "plugin-types" is obsolete: browsers no longer run plugins such as Flash or Java. You can delete it; object-src 'none' is what still matters.
deprecated.navigate-to: "navigate-to" was dropped from the specification before any browser supported it, so it has no effect. You can delete it.
deprecated.require-sri-for: "require-sri-for" never became a standard and current browsers ignore it. To check that scripts haven't changed, put integrity attributes on the script tags.

issues.ignored-in-meta: "{directive}" is ignored when the policy is set with a <meta> tag. It only works as an HTTP header.
issues.missing-quotes: "{value}" in {directive} should be written with quotes ('{value}'). Without them the browser treats it as a website name.
issues.invalid-source: "{value}" in {directive} isn't a valid value, so browsers ignore it.
issues.none-with-other-sources: {directive} contains 'none' together with other values; 'none' is then ignored.
issues.report-only-in-meta: Report-only policies can't be set with a <meta> tag; browsers ignore this one.
issues.empty-directive: {directive} has no value, which blocks everything of this type.
issues.strict-dynamic-without-nonce: {directive} has 'strict-dynamic' but no nonce or hash, so no script on the page can run. 'strict-dynamic' only trusts the scripts that a nonced or hashed script loads.
issues.placeholder-nonce: '{value}' in {directive} is the builder's placeholder. Your server must replace it with a new random value for every page it sends.
issues.hash-length: The hash '{value}' in {directive} doesn't have the right length, so it never matches any code. Copy it again in full.
issues.ignored-in-report-only: "{directive}" has no effect in a Report-Only policy: browsers ignore it there. Put it in the enforced policy.

intro.simple: If the code written in your pages rarely changes, each block can be approved one by one instead of all at once. Paste them here to get the policy to use.
intro.technical: List each inline block by its `'sha256-…'` hash. Once a hash is in the directive, browsers ignore `'unsafe-inline'` there: it stays only for very old browsers.

warning.script: Every other inline script on your pages stops running until its hash is listed, and so do `onclick="…"` attributes. Test with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first.
warning.style: Every other `<style>` block on your pages then needs its hash too. Test with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first.
warning.styleAttr: `style="…"` attributes keep working: `style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline'` is added for them.

trustedTypes.toolsNote: This policy turns on Trusted Types, and the tools picked don't say in their documentation whether they work with it. Where a tool writes HTML or loads scripts, the browser may stop it. Test with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first. [What Trusted Types change](/trusted-types)

risks.script-unsafe-inline: Code written directly in the page is allowed to run ('unsafe-inline' in {directive}). If an attacker slips code into a page, it runs too, which removes most of what the policy protects against.
risks.plain-url-schemes: {value} in {directive} lets the page load code from almost any website, so an attacker can host their code nearly anywhere.
risks.plain-wildcard: {value} in {directive} lets the page load code from any website at all, so the policy protects nothing there.

missing-directives.object-src: The policy doesn't restrict plugins (object-src). Old plugin content can be used to run code; object-src 'none' closes that door and rarely breaks anything.
missing-directives.script-src: The policy doesn't restrict scripts, so it gives no protection against injected code.
missing-directives.base-uri: The policy doesn't restrict the page's base address (base-uri). An attacker could change where the page's own scripts load from; base-uri 'none' or 'self' prevents it.

script-allowlist-bypass.open-cdn: {value} serves files anyone can publish, so an attacker could put their own code there and your policy would let it run. Allow only the libraries your site uses, by their own address.
script-allowlist-bypass.known: {value} hosts files an attacker can reuse to run their own code, so allowing it weakens the policy. Remove it if nothing on your site needs it.

object-allowlist-bypass.known: {value} in {directive} hosts files an attacker can reuse to run code through a plugin. Setting object-src to 'none' is usually possible.

findings.script-unsafe-inline: 'unsafe-inline' in {directive} lets any injected inline script or event handler run, which removes most of the protection against XSS. Nonces or hashes allow your own inline code without it.
findings.script-unsafe-hashes: 'unsafe-hashes' in {directive} allows the inline event handlers whose hashes are listed. Safer than 'unsafe-inline', but those handlers remain; moving them into script files removes the need.
findings.script-unsafe-eval: 'unsafe-eval' in {directive} lets the page turn text into code (eval(), new Function()), so injected data can end up running. Keep it only if a tool you need requires it.
findings.plain-url-schemes: {value} in {directive} allows scripts from any address with that scheme, including a site an attacker controls.
findings.plain-wildcard: {directive} allows '*', any website, so it does little against injected content.

missing-directives.object-src: Plugins (<object>, <embed>) aren't restricted, and they can run JavaScript. Set object-src 'none'.
missing-directives.script-src: Scripts aren't restricted: there is no script-src and no default-src to fall back on. This is the rule that protects against XSS.
missing-directives.base-uri: No base-uri: an injected <base> tag could send every relative script address to an attacker's server, even with nonces. Set base-uri 'none' or 'self'.

script-allowlist-bypass.open-cdn: {value} serves every package published on npm, and anyone can publish one: an attacker can put their code there and this policy lets it run. Allow only the packages you use, by their address with a path, or move to nonces with 'strict-dynamic'.
script-allowlist-bypass.known: {value} is known to host JSONP endpoints or Angular libraries that let an attacker run code despite this policy. Remove it, or move to nonces with 'strict-dynamic'.
script-allowlist-bypass.unverified: No known bypass on {value}, but if it serves JSONP replies or Angular libraries, an attacker can use it to run code. Host allowlists are hard to keep safe; nonces with 'strict-dynamic' are more robust.
script-allowlist-bypass.self: 'self' trusts every file on your own site. If it hosts JSONP endpoints, Angular or files uploaded by users, they can be used to get around the policy.

object-allowlist-bypass.known: {value} is known to host Flash files that let an attacker get around this policy. Set object-src 'none'.
object-allowlist-bypass.restrict: object-src allows {value}. Plugins are rarely needed today: can it be 'none'?

ip-source.localhost: {directive} allows localhost ({value}). Fine while developing; remove it in production.
ip-source.ip: {value} in {directive} is an IP address rather than a host name. Browsers may not match it, so it may allow nothing; use the host name.

findings.nonce-length: The nonce {value} is shorter than 8 characters and could be guessed. Generate a new random value of at least 128 bits for every response.
findings.nonce-charset: The nonce {value} uses characters outside base64. Use a base64 value.

src-http.resource: {value} in {directive} is loaded over plain HTTP, which anyone on the network can change. Use https://.
src-http.report: Violation reports are sent to {value} over plain HTTP. Use https:// so they can't be read or changed on the way.

findings.deprecated-directive: {directive} is deprecated and modern browsers ignore it.

unknown-directive.colon: Directive names don't end with a colon, so {directive} is ignored.
unknown-directive.unknown: {directive} isn't a CSP directive, so browsers ignore it.

findings.missing-semicolon: {value} in {directive} looks like a directive name, not a value. Is a semicolon missing before it?

invalid-keyword.quotes: {value} in {directive} must be written with single quotes ('{value}'). Without them it is read as a host name.
invalid-keyword.invalid: {value} in {directive} isn't a CSP keyword, so it is ignored.

ignored.unsafe-inline: 'unsafe-inline' in {directive} is ignored because the rule also has a nonce or a hash. It only matters for very old browsers.
ignored.strict-dynamic: {value} in {directive} is ignored because of 'strict-dynamic': only scripts with the nonce or hash, and the scripts they load, run.

notice.nonceChanged: The nonce differs between the two, as it should: a new one for every page. It isn't counted as a change.

start.nonceQuestion: Can your site add a nonce to each page?

nonceExplain.simple: A nonce is a one-time code your server writes into each page and into its `<script>` tags. Only scripts carrying it run. Ask your developers: if they're not sure, choose **No**.
nonceExplain.developer: A fresh random value per response, sent in the policy and set as the `nonce` attribute of every `<script>`. With `'strict-dynamic'`, scripts loaded by a nonced script are trusted too, so tag managers keep working.
nonceExplain.security: A nonce with `'strict-dynamic'` resists the allowlist bypasses that affect host-based policies (JSONP, open redirects, script gadgets on allowed CDNs). It needs server-side rendering or an edge function to inject the value.

start.nonceHint: The strongest option: scripts run only if your page vouches for them.
start.olderBrowsersHint: Adds `'unsafe-inline' https:` for browsers too old for `'strict-dynamic'` (before 2022). Current browsers ignore both, so they stay as protected.
start.allowlistHint: Scripts are trusted by where they come from. Simpler to run, easier to bypass.

site.question: Your pages
site.unsure: Not sure? Leave it unticked: the browser console will name what's blocked when you test the policy.
site.addressHint: Used to check what 'self' covers. Leave it empty if you prefer.

unrestricted.script: Your policy has no `script-src` or `default-src` yet: nothing restricts scripts, so every inline script already runs and these hashes change nothing. Start from a blank policy, or add one of those lines to your own.
unrestricted.style: Your policy has no `style-src` or `default-src` yet: nothing restricts styles, so every inline style already applies and these hashes change nothing. Start from a blank policy, or add one of those lines to your own.

script.simple: Paste each one below. Only these exact blocks will run: when one changes, its hash must be updated in the policy too.
script.technical: Each block is listed by its `'sha256-…'` hash. Once a hash is in `script-src`, browsers ignore `'unsafe-inline'` there: every inline script needs its hash, and `onclick="…"` attributes stop working.

style.simple: Paste each one below. Only these exact blocks will apply: when one changes, its hash must be updated in the policy too.
style.technical: Each block is listed by its `'sha256-…'` hash. Once a hash is in `style-src`, browsers ignore `'unsafe-inline'` there: every `<style>` block needs its hash, and `style="…"` attributes get `style-src-attr` of their own.

inline-scripts.label: Have code written directly in the page
inline-scripts.hint: <script> blocks with code inside, such as a tag snippet pasted into the page.
inline-scripts.detail: Inline <script> elements. Allowed with 'unsafe-inline', or with the nonce.

inline-handlers.label: Use onclick="…" attributes
inline-handlers.hint: Buttons or links with code in an attribute. Common in older sites and some themes.
inline-handlers.detail: Inline event handlers (script-src-attr). A nonce can't cover them: only 'unsafe-inline' or 'unsafe-hashes'.

eval.label: Run code built from text
eval.hint: Some older libraries and templates do this. Rare in modern sites.
eval.detail: eval(), new Function() or setTimeout with a string. Needs 'unsafe-eval'.

inline-styles.label: Have styles written directly in the page
inline-styles.hint: <style> blocks inside the page, common with page builders.
inline-styles.detail: Inline <style> elements. Allowed with 'unsafe-inline', or with the nonce.

style-attributes.label: Use style="…" attributes
style-attributes.hint: Elements styled one by one, common with page builders and rich-text content.

data-images.label: Show images written as data: addresses
data-images.hint: Small icons embedded in the code instead of loaded as files.
data-images.detail: data: URLs in img-src. Low risk for images.

inline-script.one: A script written in the page

inline-style.other: {count} style blocks written in the page

what.inline-handler: An event handler written in the page (`onclick`, `onload`…)

trusted.TrustedHTML: HTML written into the page as plain text
trusted.TrustedScriptURL: A script address set as plain text
trusted.unknown: Plain text handed to the browser where it needs a Trusted Type

violations.reported: Not blocked: your report-only policy reported it under `{directive}`.
violations.fallback: Your policy has no `{effective}`, so the browser used `{directive}`.
violations.noTool: No tool in the catalogue uses this address. Check what it is before allowing it: part of your site, a tool the catalogue doesn't have yet, or code a browser extension added to the page.
violations.noToolReport: No tool in the catalogue uses this address, and it isn't on your site's domain.
violations.createdNote: Your policy has no `{directive}` yet, so the browser used `default-src`. This new rule starts with the values of `default-src`, so nothing else changes.
violations.fixAddCreated: Add a `{directive}` rule to your policy: the values of your `default-src`, then `{add}`.
violations.reportOnlyFix: Make this change in your report-only policy, so that it doesn't block this once you enforce it.
violations.evalTools: In the catalogue, these need it: {tools}.
violations.hash: The browser gave this code's hash. Adding it allows this exact code and nothing else: if the code changes, it's blocked again. For code that changes on each page, [use a nonce](/nonces) instead.
violations.noHash: This browser doesn't give the code's hash. Paste the code below to get it, or [use a nonce](/nonces).
violations.noHashReport: Reports don't carry the code's hash, and their sample is cut at 40 characters. Paste the code below to get it, or [use a nonce](/nonces).
violations.styleAttr: The safest way is to move these styles into your stylesheet, as classes: then nothing in your policy has to change. Styles a script sets (`element.style.color = …`) aren't blocked either.
violations.handler: The safest way is to move this code into a script and attach it with `addEventListener`: then nothing in your policy has to change.
violations.extension: `{host}` is a browser extension installed where this message appeared, not part of your site. Nothing to change in your policy.
violations.extensionReport: `{host}` is a browser extension installed by one of your visitors, not part of your site. Nothing to change in your policy.
violations.ancestors: The page at {host} doesn't allow other sites to show it in a frame (its `frame-ancestors` rule). Only its owner can change that: your policy has nothing to do with it.

lines.title: What to change in your policy
lines.intro: Copy them all: each one replaces the rule of the same name in your policy. Together they allow what these messages say was blocked, and nothing else.
lines.add: Add this rule to your policy
lines.replaceReportOnly: In your report-only policy, replace your {directive} rule with
lines.addReportOnly: Add this rule to your report-only policy

violations.tt: Your policy requires Trusted Types (`require-trusted-types-for`): code can't hand the browser {what} as plain text, only through a Trusted Types policy that checks it first. The code that did this, your own or a tool's, has to use one. There is nothing to add to your policy for it: [how Trusted Types work](/trusted-types).
violations.ttTool: The text you pasted has an address used by [{vendor}](/vendors/{id}). If its code is the one blocked, ask {vendor} whether it supports Trusted Types.
violations.evalBest: The safest way is code that doesn't build code from text: check whether the library or tool has a version without `eval`, or ask the people who make it.
violations.schemeBest: The safest way is to load this code from a file at an address, on your site or the tool's: then nothing made in the page can run as a script.
violations.inlineIgnored: Your `{directive}` rule has a nonce or a hash, so browsers ignore `'unsafe-inline'` there: a hash or a nonce is the only way to allow this code.

risk.eval: `'unsafe-eval'` lets every script on the page run code built from text, which also makes an injected script easier to run. Use it only for a tool you trust that has no other way.
risk.scheme: `{add}` in `{directive}` lets scripts come from content made in the page, which an attacker who slips text into the page can make too.
risk.inline-script: `'unsafe-inline'` in `{directive}` lets every script written in the page run, including one an attacker slips in through a form, a comment or a hacked tool: it turns off most of what your policy protects against. Use it only for a short while, until you have hashes or a nonce.
risk.inline-style: `'unsafe-inline'` in `{directive}` lets every style written in the page apply, including styles an attacker slips in, which can hide or fake parts of the page and leak what it shows. Scripts stay protected.
risk.style-attr: This lets every `style` attribute apply, including one an attacker slips in, which can hide or fake parts of the page. Scripts and style blocks stay protected, and a style attribute can't run code.
risk.handler: This lets every event handler written in the page run, including one an attacker slips in (``): that's how most injected code runs. `

weaker.replaceReportOnly: If you accept that, replace your {directive} rule in your report-only policy with
weaker.addReportOnly: If you accept that, add this rule to your report-only policy

violations.hashFold: Get the hash from the code
violations.noHashPaper: Reports don't carry the code's hash, and their sample is cut at 40 characters: get the hash from the code itself (the [reports reader](/reports) has a tool for it), or [use a nonce](/nonces).

reportsReader.hint: JSON as browsers send it (report-to or report-uri), one report per line from your logs, or your collector's export in JSON or CSV. Or drop the file here.

error.tooLarge: This file is too large to read here (more than {max}). Export fewer days, or only the reports with `csp-violation`.
error.unreadable: This file couldn't be read. Is it a text file?

reportsReader.noneLong: No CSP violation report found in this text. A report says what was blocked (a `blockedURL` or `blocked-uri` field, or a column of that name in a CSV export) and under which rule: paste them as your collector stored or exported them.

noiseLead.one: 1 report wasn't caused by your site: it is set apart at the end, with why.
noiseLead.other: {count} reports weren't caused by your site: they are set apart at the end, by cause.

skipped.one: 1 line held something other than a report and was left out.
skipped.other: {count} lines held something other than a report and were left out.

reportsReader.linesIntro: Each line replaces the rule of the same name in the policy that sent the reports. Together they allow the problems above that point to them, and nothing else.
reportsReader.compare: See the whole policy with these changes, in the comparator
reportsReader.unknown: It could be a tool someone added without telling you, or code slipped into your pages: a hacked plugin or tool, or malware on a visitor's device. So it isn't in the lines. Before allowing it, find what loads it: search your site's code and your tag manager for `{host}`.
reportsReader.trust: I know what this is: allow it in the lines
reportsReader.guessed: Safari's older reports don't say whether a policy was enforced or report-only: these are taken as enforced.

extension.intro: Extensions your visitors installed add code to the pages they visit, and your policy blocks it. That's your policy doing its job: there is nothing to allow.
extension.name: Browser extensions

software.intro: Antivirus software, programs that inject ads and company proxies add code to every page their users open, and your policy blocks it. Their addresses are well known. Nothing to allow: it isn't part of your site.
software.name: Software on visitors' devices

translation.intro: When visitors translate your page (Chrome's built-in translation, or a translated copy on `translate.goog`), the translator adds its own styles and scripts. Nothing to allow: it's the visitor's tool, not your site's, and your page still works in its own language.
translation.name: Translation

in-app.intro: Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and other apps open links in a browser of their own, which adds its own code to the page. Only such browsers reported these: your site doesn't load them itself.
in-app.name: Apps' built-in browsers

bot.intro: Search engines' crawlers, monitoring and test tools, and scrapers. Only they reported these, no visitor's browser did. If one of them is your own monitoring, check its setup rather than your policy.
bot.name: Bots

copy.intro: These came from your pages shown somewhere else: a search engine's cache, an archive, a page saved on someone's computer. The copy keeps your policy but not your address, so things break there that work on your site.
copy.name: Copies of your pages

browser.intro: Browsers' own pages and internal addresses (`about:`, `chrome://`, `resource://`…) sometimes end up in reports. They aren't part of your site.
browser.name: The browser itself

undated.one: 1 report without a date left out.
undated.other: {count} reports without a date left out.

names.title: Trusted Types policies your rule refuses
names.text: Code tried to create Trusted Types policies named {names}, which your `trusted-types` rule doesn't list. If they are yours or a tool's you trust, add their names to that rule ([how Trusted Types work](/trusted-types)).

policies.intro: Reports carry the whole policy the page was sent. Several policies: an enforced and a report-only one, pages with their own, or an older version still in some browsers.

replaced.one: Policy {n}, an older version: 1 report, until {date}
replaced.other: Policy {n}, an older version: {count} reports, until {date}

policies.replacedIntro: Reports from an older version are read against the newest policy in these reports: what it allows is marked “Allowed since” in the list.

guessed.one: Policy {n}, enforced or report-only (Safari didn't say): 1 report
guessed.other: Policy {n}, enforced or report-only (Safari didn't say): {count} reports

policies.missing: The reports didn't include the policy.

risk.unknown: an address no known tool uses
risk.sensitive: on {page}, where visitors pay or sign in
risk.reported: only reported, nothing is blocked yet
risk.code: it runs code or sends data
risk.look: it only changes how the page looks
risk.stopped: not seen since {date}, maybe already fixed

unknownWide.one: an address no known tool uses, but on 1 page since the reports start
unknownWide.other: an address no known tool uses, but on {count} pages since the reports start: more likely a tool someone added than code slipped in

enforce.title: Can you enforce it?

notYet.one: **Not yet.** Once enforced, this report-only policy would block 1 thing your site uses: the problem below.
notYet.other: **Not yet.** Once enforced, this report-only policy would block {count} things your site uses: the problems below.

inLines.one: The lines below allow 1 of them.
inLines.other: The lines below allow {count} of them.

enforce.allInLines: The lines below allow all of them.

needsWork.one: 1 needs a change in your code or a check first: it says how.
needsWork.other: {count} need a change in your code or a check first: each one says how.

enforce.notYetNext: Put the lines in your report-only policy, deal with the rest, then collect reports again for a week. When only what's set apart comes in, it's ready.
enforce.tooSoon: **Nothing your site uses would be blocked, but it's too soon to say.**
enforce.tooSoonDays: These reports cover {days}. Collect them for at least a week: pages people open less often (account pages, campaigns, a monthly email) may not have spoken yet.
enforce.tooSoonUndated: These reports have no dates, so there's no telling how long they cover. Collect them for at least a week: pages people open less often (account pages, campaigns, a monthly email) may not have spoken yet.
enforce.ready: **It looks ready.** Over {days}, its reports show nothing your site uses that it would block.

readyNoise.one: The 1 report left is set apart below: not your site's doing.
readyNoise.other: The {count} reports left are set apart below: not your site's doing.

readySteps.header: Send it as `Content-Security-Policy` instead of `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, with the same `report-to`, so you still hear about anything missed.
readySteps.unseen: Check by hand what reports can't speak for: pages nobody opened in these days, like an admin area or a rare form.
readySteps.next: Keep a report-only copy for your next change, and try it there first.

reportsReader.fixedIntro: The policy your pages sent from {date} allows it, and no report about it came after that. If it's still the policy your site sends, there's nothing to do. If more reports come, some pages or browsers still get the older one.
reportsReader.linesFrom: What to change in the policy sent from {date}
reportsReader.linesForFrom: What to change in policy {n}, sent from {date}

noiseTitle.one: Set apart: 1 report your site didn't cause
noiseTitle.other: Set apart: {count} reports your site didn't cause

include.pages: Include the pages of each problem
include.policies: Include the policies in the reports
include.samples: Include what the reports quoted of the code

save.hint: Made in your browser from what this page shows: nothing is sent, and the reports themselves aren't in it. A day picked in “Only the reports since” and the addresses you marked as known are said in it.

document.title: Violation reports

vouched.one: 1 address no known tool uses was marked as known, and is in the lines.
vouched.other: {count} addresses no known tool uses were marked as known, and are in the lines.

document.footer: Read in the browser with {site}: the reports never left it.

own.one: 1 domain counted as the site's own: {sites}.
own.other: {count} domains counted as the site's own: {sites}.

own.added: {site} counted as one of your domains: its addresses are in the lines.
own.removed: {site} no longer counted as one of your domains.

quotes.samples: The start of the blocked code, as browsers quoted it:
quotes.note: Browsers quote at most the first 40 characters: enough to recognise your own code, or code you didn't write.
quotes.sources: The script that was running when it happened:
quotes.none: These reports don't quote the blocked code: add `'report-sample'` to your `{directive}` rule, and the next ones will show its first 40 characters, enough to tell your own code from code slipped in.
